discovery: The titanium-sapphire laser and passive mode-locking (Kerr-lens and SESAM) that made robust femtosecond solid-state lasers possible
motivation: Moulton's invention of the Ti:sapphire laser (1982) provided a gain medium with enormous bandwidth. Sibbett's discovery of self-mode-locking via the Kerr lens (1991) and Keller's semiconductor saturable absorber mirror (1992) turned that bandwidth into reliable, turnkey femtosecond pulses. These simple, clever ideas removed the dye laser as a barrier and made ultrafast lasers practical in ordinary laboratories. Nearly every high-intensity system built on chirped pulse amplification, along with optical frequency combs, attosecond sources, femtochemistry, multiphoton microscopy and precision micromachining, starts with a mode-locked solid-state oscillator traceable to this work. Physics prizes have repeatedly honoured discoveries made with these lasers. The enabling laser science underneath them has gone unrecognised for more than three decades, and it deserves the Prize.
